content.title: Interesting and simple architectural change, but it seems to have rather marginal effects and the experiments should be more extensive.
content.review:
Summary 
The paper introduces "hierarchical binding" an extension of CNN architectures that uses feature unpooling to keep track of which low-level features drive the activation of high-level features. The experimental results demonstrate that this simple architectural extension leads to a slightly increased robustness w.r.t. a variety of adversarial attacks, for a limited range of architectures and on simple datasets. 

Pros 
+ The proposed approach is simple yet seems effective
+ The paper is well written and presents the proposed approach clearly
+ The experiments involve a range of different types of attacks

Criticism
- The proposed is simple and does not involve any theoretical contributions (the methods section comprises one short paragraph). While this is not necessarily negative, it requires the experiments to be a very extensive empirical study in order to generate a strong enough contribution. However, the experiments in the paper only involve a LeNet architecture tested on MNIST. This is a significant limitation. More experiments are presented in the appendix, however, these also only involve simple datasets (FMNIST,CIFAR) and outdated architectures (VGG). To make a convincing argument about the general 
applicability of the proposed approach it is necessary to show that it also generalizes to modern architectures and complex datasets with higher resolution images. 
- The increase in the robustness of the proposed architecture is rather low. The final model is still very vulnerable to adversarial attacks compared to a standard CNN (CNN+S+N).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Post rebuttal:

Thank you for your brief answer to some of my comments. My major concern remains that the experimental evaluation is limited and should be much more extensive because the theoretical contribution is limited. I think the paper is not ready for publication yet. Therefore, I keep my initial rating.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Not convinced that evaluation of adversarial robustness can be trusted; results beyond MNIST are underwhelming
content.review:
UPDATE AFTER REBUTTAL

I have read the authors response. However, the results remain underwhelming and the lack of a demonstration on a larger dataset is a crucial issue in my opinion. Therefore I stand by my assessment.


ORIGINAL REVIEW

The paper proposes a method of achieving adversarial robustness by focussing on the mechanism that combines features from different spatial locations (feature binding). The authors argue that invariant feature representations causes class manifolds to become overly simple, neglecting details. According to the authors, this leads to tight (close to object manifold) decision boundaries, which have arbitrary shape outside the class manifold. Hence, by manipulating details which are not captured by class manifolds the decision boundary can easily be crossed, i.e an adversarial sample is found. To prevent this, the authors suggest the novel hierarchical binding (HB-CNN) architecture. Instead of propagating max-pooled activations only, subsequent layers are additionally given the spatial positions the max-pooled activation originated from.


Strengths:
+ Evaluation of a large number of attacks using L_0, L_2 and L_inf distances
+ Investigation of three datasets: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10
+ Significantly more efficient method for adversarial robustness than competitors


Weaknesses:
- Evaluation of robustness seems to suffer from severe optimization issues
- Results on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 are underwhelming compared to MNIST
- Relation to feature binding in the brain is unclear
- Some crucial details about model architecture are missing


Details on major issues (all of which would need to be addressed in a convincing manner for my score to change):

(1) Evaluation of robustness seems to suffer from severe optimization issues

The median of half the L2 distance to the closest sample of a different class on MNIST is ~2.9. The authors claim a median L2 distance of successful adversaries of 3.4 for their method, which is implausible: simply finding the closest sample from a different class and linearly interpolating would make for a stronger attack. 

The authors may need to run many more iterations (25–1000x) for the boundary attack, tune the step size or run multiple random initializations when attacking. In addition, more recent strong attacks like DDN attack, AutoAttack, BrendelBethge attack are missing from the evaluation. These issues cast serious doubt on the effectiveness of the method and would have to be resolved before the paper can be published.


(2) Results on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 are underwhelming compared to MNIST

These results should not be hidden in the appendix. On these datasets, the method underperforms by quite a margin. It could be argued that the method is more efficient, but if it's not effective, I am not sure what's the value of efficiency. As it stands, I am not convinced of the value of the method.

Results on ImageNet (or a smaller subset of it) could make the paper more convincing, in particular as the network is simple and computational efficiency is claimed in the conclusion.


(3) Relation to feature binding in the brain is unclear

I could not follow the reasoning what this approach has to do with feature binding -- and I think the paper does not need this story. You might as well explain what the method is doing without the reference to neuroscience, which is weak at best.


(4) Some crucial details about model architecture are missing

I think the model description of HB-CNN (Sec. 3) could be improved. While the local mechanism is well explained, I am missing a more detailed description of how this local block integrated in the network. 

For the VGG-based architecture used for CIFAR-10 the integration of hierarchical binding is unclear. Is it applied at multiple layers? If yes, how are the differently shaped outputs integrated?


Minor comments

- I suggest to move Fig. 6 from appendix to main paper, because it helps understanding how the local block presented in Fig. 2 is integrated into LeNet-5.

- As far as I can tell, HB specifically addresses pooling and striding. This should be clearly stated in the abstract and introduction.

- The well-known SegNet architecture relies on unpooling but is missing from literature discussion (Badrinarayanan et al.: "Segnet: A deep convolutional encoder-decoder architecture for image segmentation.").

- The only state-of-the-art baseline presented in the tables is CNN+AT, i.e. Madry et al. (2018). Performance in relation to Schott et al. (2019) is discussed in the text but not considered a fair comparison. The line of reasoning here is not clear to me. Why are the numbers not comparable?

- Wouldn't it be sufficient to indicate the unpooled position only and ignore its value, which is the output of max-pool anyway. This means, in Fig. 2a, the output of unpool could be [[1,0],[0,0]] instead of [[8,0],[0,0]] without loss of information. The sample should apply for gradient unpool, since the convolutional filter is known.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Re. unpooling and comparing to Schott et al

content.title: Re. unpooling and comparing to Schott et al
content.comment:
Many thanks for your comments, in particular the advice given on improving the attacks leveraged – please see our general comment addressing this, as well as hopefully a clearer explanation of the significance of the representations we are using, and their connection to the primate visual cortex.

-	Re. simply providing the position as a 1 without activation values, we also considered this, but decided on our current implementation as a) with a linear read-out, a binary unpooled value would be constrained to act as a bias, whereas including its activation allows the positional encoding to influence the slope of the function and b) setting the values to 1 would prevent useful gradients during learning. 

-	Thank you for your comment re. SegNet by Badrinarayanan et al – in addition to adding this reference, we are adding a reference to Xu et al, 2019, who used a modified form of unpooling (‘ratio unpooling’) in a feed-forward architecture to preserve spatial information, but which we excluded from the first submission due to space constraints. 

-	Our comment that our results may not be completely comparable to Schott et al was a concession on our part – we were simply noting that e.g. the MNIST subset used for evaluation and the adversaries used for transfer attacks were different, and so it may be that, were this controlled for, our stronger performance might not be as large as we reported. 

Reference:

Chunyan Xu, Jian Yang, Hanjiang Lai, Junbin Gao, Linlin Shen, & Shuicheng Yan (2019). UP-CNN: Un-pooling augmented convolutional neural network. Pattern Recognition Letters.

content.title: interesting architecture for feature binding, but lacking clarity in the results
content.review:
This paper presents a neuroscience inspired architecture that incorporates hierarchical binding as a way to bind the low-level and high-level features of an input representation. The authors hypothesize that this binding will help constrain the network to have fewer off-manifold adversarial examples, and demonstrate that this is the case when the architecture is combined with label smoothing and noisy training data.  

My main concern about the paper is in the clarity of the presented results. The idea behind a hierarchical binding model is compelling, however it is difficult to separate out the contribution of  this model for adversarial robustness from the (less novel) label smoothing and added noise.

Positives: 			
* The geometric intuition behind the defense (particularly as laid out in Figure 1) is very interesting. 
* The neuroscience inspired unpooling-based hierarchical binding architecture is novel as a way to incorporate representations from multiple spatial scales. 
* The paper presents a thorough analysis of many different adversarial attacks to compare the different presented methods
* The authors provide discussion and analysis of how gradient obfuscation is likely not the reason for the robustness that they observed.  	
	
Concerns and Questions: 
* The results are difficult to interpret, specifically separating out the effect of the hierarchical binding from the label-smoothing results (where the label smoothing results are not a novel contribution). It appears that Table 1 only includes results on the boundary attack -- the text says that the model is not more resistant to typical attacks such as transfer attacks but quantification of these results appears to be missing from the paper. Further, all of the models (except the AT model) in Table 2 seem to include label smoothing. 
* Similar to the above, the paper does not present results for an HBCNN+N (or control CNN+N) model, so it is not possible to separate out the effect of adding noise alone from the additive effect of smoothing plus noise. Especially given that label smoothing produced inconsistent results across the different attacks, is label smoothing helping more than just including noisy training data? 
* Given the importance of label smoothing to the main results, the paper would be more clear by introducing the concept in the introduction or related work (rather than just introducing in the experiment section)
* How does the robustness due to hierarchical binding compare with other ways of preserving low-level information (ie ResNet or I-RevNet, as mentioned in the paper)? The authors claim that their result is novel in that it “captures which low-level neurons causally drove high-level representations”, but it is unclear whether it is this causality, or simply a preservation of multiple spatial scales, that is driving the observed robustness.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

display_title: the motivation seems unjustified and results need more work

content.title: the motivation seems unjustified and results need more work
content.review:
This paper proposes a new architecture for CNNs that is more robust against adversarial attacks. The main argument of the paper seems to be about the low-dimensionality of the existing CNN representational spaces that lead to loss of low-level details at the classification level. This paper is an attempt to resolve this hypothetical issue. 

Overall, my main concerns were regarding 1. the correctness of the claimed relationship between representational dimensionality and adversarial robustness and 2. the effectiveness of the proposed method considering the presented results. 

* The authors motivate their work by claiming that the existence of adversarial examples is partly due to the low-dimensional representation in CNNs and that this is in contrast to the representations in the brain. This claim which seems central to the argument underlying the proposed architecture is very unintuitive to me since all CNNs retain the information about the features in their feature maps. Architectures with skip connections like ResNet and DenseNet additionally propagate the early feature maps to later layers too. However all of these networks still suffer from the adversarial examples. In addition, as far as I know the object representation in the primate brain has low-dimensionality [1] which is even smaller than those found in the higher levels of CNNs. 
Related to this point, some statements in the paper like: page1, par2, sentence3 and figure-1 caption seem unjustified to me because they tie the lack of explicit low-level information to adversarial robustness. 
The results in Fig3 are presented as evidence of “causal” role of the binding dimension on robustness but despite this these results don’t seem to portray in clear picture of such relationship. With increasing \gamma parameter the L-inf distance seem to initially improve but remains unchanged for most of the range and then finally decreased. The possible explanations for the reduction with high \gamma don’t seem logical to me. 

* Based on the results presented in Table-2 the proposed HBCNN architecture seems to be effective at improving adversarial robustness on MNIST dataset compared to the original CNN. One of the concerns with this comparison is the indirect effect that the proposed architectural change has on the size of the network. The authors have provided additional experiments in the appendix that aims to rule out this effect as the main driver of this effect however there is no description of how the network sizes were matched in this experiment. In addition, unlike the MNIST results, the improvement on Fashion-MNIST and Cifar10 results seem to be less evident as the improvements are mostly small or non-existent. This raises some concerns on the applicability of the proposed architecture on more meaningful datasets like Cifar10. It would also be helpful to see the results of network size matching for these experiments. Also I feel that fashion-MNIST and Cifar10 results should be part of the main manuscript instead of being pushed back to the appendix. 

Other comments: 
* what implementation was used for adversarial training? please include more details about the attack used during training 
* the specifications of each of the attacks are missing (e.g. number of iterations for deepfool)
* PGD attacks are visibly missing from the reported results. 
* It would be interesting to see whether combining the proposed architecture with adversarial training would lead to an additive effect in robustness or not. 
* authors point to table-1 for results showing "the new model is no more resistant to typical attacks" but table-1 does not contain this result
* Confidence intervals should be shown on results in all tables specially for the results with very close values across architectures
* figure captions look like they are part of the text — they should be reformatted 
 
[1] Lehky, S. R., Kiani, R., Esteky, H., & Tanaka, K. (2014). Dimensionality of object representations in monkey inferotemporal cortex. Neural computation, 26(10), 2135-2162.

**************************
Update after the rebuttal: 

I thank the authors for providing a response to my comments. The authors' responses did not convince me on the arguments about the relationship between dimensionality and adversarial robustness. I still find the Cifar10 results unimpressive and several of my other comments still remain unanswered. Overall, my opinion about the paper has not significantly changed after the rebuttal and I keep my previous score.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Common Response to All Reviewers
content.comment:
We would like to thank all of the reviewers for their time and valuable comments. In the interest of avoiding repetition, below are general comments, while specific questions will be addressed individually. 

### Re. the question of the dimensionality of human/primate representations

It is clear that many aspects of primate vision rely primarily on abstract, low-dimensional representations, which is consistent with our proposal here, and that vision can be impoverished e.g. outside of attention. What we are describing here however is the primate perception of “objects along with their detailed features” (Lu et al, 2018). For example, even in the periphery, humans are sensitive to low-level image changes when these impact scene-like content as opposed to textures (Wallis et al, 2019). Primates have access to such low/mid-level information in higher processing, such as local border ownership (Kim et al, 2009). Thus the representations we’ve described are consistent with “vision with scrutiny”, rather than coarse object recognition (Hochstein, 2002). The work cited by one of the reviewers from Lehky et al, 2014 estimating low-dimensional representations in primate visual cortex is compatible with our proposal here, as they measured neural activity in anterior inferotemporal cortex. Based on current evidence, it is likely that the neural binding representations would be predominantly distributed in lower-levels of the visual cortex (Zhou et al 2000, Lu et al, 2018). 


### Re. the connection of adversarial robustness to hierarchical binding and neuroscience generally

Humans without time-constraints do not appear to be sensitive to adversarial perturbations (see e.g. recent limitations identified by Dujmovic et al, 2020 regarding Zhou et al, 2019), and as such the only experimental evidence for human sensitivity to adversarial examples is from Elsayed et al, 2018. While the effect on classification was not comparable to the dramatic shift seen in machine vision systems, they measured significant drops in accuracy when humans were constrained to view adversarial images for a very short duration (around 60-70ms) followed by masking intended to limit recurrent and top-down processing. However, the introduction of recurrent activity in a model designed to better match the primate ventral stream (CORNet-S) is not associated with enhanced robustness – in fact the base CORNet-S  architecture used in Dapello et al, 2020 was more vulnerable than AlexNet to adversarial examples (see their Figure 2b). Given that recurrence in a convolutional neural network is not sufficient to enable robustness, this raises the question of what specific computation was actually hindered experimentally in Elsayad to explain their results. As noted in our main text, it has been predicted that top-down and lateral activity in a spiking neural network would be needed to implement the proposed hierarchical binding algorithm, and so this provides an alternative hypothesis for the observed effect.

There have been some valuable contributions to explain human robustness to adversarial examples, but we feel these still leave important questions unanswered. Vuyyuru et al, 2020 examined the effect of non-uniform retinal sampling and varying receptive field sizes with eccentricity, which could certainly contribute to human robustness, but their effect was specific to small perturbations, and the evaluation of black-box attacks was limited, with no comparison of whether transfer attack robustness was greater for the proposed model vs. an undefended one. Tadros et al, 2020 examined the effect of sleep-like algorithms on robustness, and again while this might account for some of the difference between humans and artificial systems, their method actually increased the vulnerability of the model on MNIST to the Boundary Attack (see their Table 1), with no evaluation of other black-box methods such as transfer attacks or the Pointwise attack. Finally, in Dapello et al, 2020, various aspects of early primate visual processing were explored as defence methods, but the primary benefit was accounted for by V1 stochasticity (see their Figure 3), and again there was no analysis of transfer attacks. In summary, we feel there is still a significant explanatory gap re. human robustness to adversarial examples, in particular to transfer attacks – the one method that has been leveraged against humans, and the threat setting where we feel our method performs particularly well. We therefore felt it important to make the connection to neuroscience, in particular connecting the representations in the primate brain to robustness. We will make this motivation and connection clearer in a new section of the appendix.

(response continued below)

replying_to: Replying to Common Response to All Reviewers

content.title: Common response pt. 2
content.comment:
### Re. other architectures that preserve low-level information

The importance of hierarchical binding is that the low-level features are always represented explicitly, with their own activations and thereby unique learned weights to the decision part of the network – architectures using skip connections, in contrast, combine information from low and high level layers in an operation that can obscure their respective contributions and makes classifier read-out of the low-level details more challenging. Our approach is related to the motivation for (and biological evidence of) disentangled/untangled representations (e.g. Gaspar et al, 2019) - our goal is “to disentangle as many factors as possible, discarding as little information about the data as is practical” (Bengio, 2013). Thus the architecture is designed to avoid the more entangled representation of detailed and abstract features than would be found in ResNets and related architectures such as i-RevNet. Returning to our initial proposal and Figure 1 of our submission, the motivation here is to enable the model to have sufficient representational capacity as well as amenable features to learn decision boundaries along all dimensions that constitute class-preserving transformations of the object. This then brings in the importance of developing a sparse representation of the low-level features that were causally involved (by our approximate measure) in the high-level representation – the classifier should be influenced by dimensions that describe the object, not noise contributed by other low-level feature detectors that may be co-active (Ahmad, 2019). The purpose of Figure 3 is to show that explicitly providing all the low-level information, including this ‘feature-noise’, is still better than not providing it at all. It is unsurprising however that increasing gamma towards 1.0 will lead to a modest drop in robustness with the inclusion of these uninformative features vs. a sparse representation. In summary, the desire is not to preserve all information in the image through an entangled representation (which deep-invertible networks do perfectly), but rather to create useful representations for a robust classifier by explicitly encoding the abstract and low-level features of an object. Hierarchical binding through the causal significance of a unit helps ensure it is only the relevant features that are actually represented. This is thus orthogonal to and compatible with the benefits of skip connections. We predict that ResNets alone would benefit less from the combination of label smoothing and noise than our own architecture (ResNets undergo a significant reduction in manifold dimensionality as the fully connected component of the network is approached - Cohen et al, 2020 Supplementary Materials), although we acknowledge the limitation of having not yet compared these directly. 

### Re. attack evaluations

Regarding our choice of attack evaluations, we had intended to replicate what we viewed to be one of the most thorough assessments in the literature of adversarial robustness (that conducted by Schott et al), while also working within the constraints of our implementation in the Foolbox 2.4 repository/TensorFlow 1.1x. We also acknowledge the limitations of the attack optimizations performed however, given the reported L-2 robustness of 3.4 on MNIST – thank you for pointing this out. We have been doing what we can to port our work to PyTorch/Foolbox 3 (which is necessary for the BrendelBethge and DDN attacks, although note that Foolbox 3 lacks other attacks we have evaluated, such as the Pointwise attacks), although this has presented some challenges. We have therefore performed PGD attacks with multiple random starts (these were excluded from the original analysis due to our inclusion of BIM, and in line with Schott et al) – searching over step sizes and number of iterations (including up to 1000) we arrived at an initial step-size of 0.01, 250 iterations, and 20 random starts. These have enabled us to provide a more reasonable PGD L-2 robustness of 2.8 on MNIST for the HB-CNN+N+S, vs 2.5 for LeNet+S+N – we will include these results and the new All L-2 and All L-Inf results in our updated Table 1. We have also conducted further evaluations with the Boundary attack as suggested by one of the reviewers, the results of which are included below. These results are from using  the first HBCNN+S+N model of the 30 we trained, which happened to have a below-average robustness to the Boundary attack. We report the median L-2 distance when using the strongest hyper-parameters.

Baseline (1,000 iterations, step adaptation size = 1.5) :	 6.18

25,000 iterations, step adaptation size = 1.1 :	 6.05

100,000 iterations, step adaptation size = 1.1 : 	5.75

1,000,000 iterations, step adaptation size = 1.01 :		5.64

As can be seen, some marginal improvement is observed, but the results are not competitive with other attack methods.

content.title: Common response pt. 3
content.comment:
### Re. attack evaluations (continued)

We agree with one of the reviewers that some estimate of uncertainty for the attack results which were close would be helpful. These were excluded from our tables as there is already a large amount of information being presented to the reader in these, so we are including separate histograms in the updated submission where results are close, such as the Pointwise attacks.

It’s possible that a more advanced attack method or e.g. even more random starts to PGD would find better adversaries than the attacks we’ve leveraged - our proposal cannot guarantee the absence of vulnerable spaces in the decision boundary, it rather aims to reduce the number of directions in which these are found. Our results show however that the model is more robust across a variety of methods and distance measures, in particular to transfer attacks, i.e. when using directions that are successful against other models, supporting the notion of fewer vulnerable dimensions (Tramer, 2017). 

### Re. demonstrating with complex datasets and modern architectures:

The concept of adversarial examples as manifold failures has had appeal for some time, but defences in this area have either been a) limited to toy datasets (Tanay et al, 2016), or b) required the use of generative models, some of which are limited to MNIST (Schott et al, 2019). We therefore propose that a significant contribution of this work is to show a method at least working in principle on more complex data-sets that does not rely on generative models. Outside of this area, leading methods such as adversarial training, favoured for its generalization to difficult real-world tasks such as ImageNet, also introduce enhanced vulnerabilities, which our approach does not (see Schott et al Table 1 or our updated version, note in particular the performance of the adversarially trained network on the L-2 Pointwise attack and L-0 based attacks on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST vs the vanilla LeNet model). In other words, robustness to certain attacks frequently introduces vulnerability to others, whereas with the exception of low-threat settings such as salt-and-pepper noise, our method either enhances robustness or maintains it at a consistent level vs. the control. Thus robustness even on simple tasks remains an outstanding issue. We agree that the effect-size on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 is small, and that the lack of demonstration with a ResNet architecture on ImageNet is unsatisfying – we believe however that this work still represents a useful contribution to the field in understanding adversarial examples as a failure of representation learning.

### Summary

We believe the importance of this paper is a) the connection of adversarial robustness to representation dimensionality, specifically that in the primate brain due to hierarchical binding b) the relevance of this to the disparity in adversarial robustness between humans and convolutional neural networks, in particular to transfer attacks, and c) a (first-step) method to practically implementing a solution based on this relationship. 
 
### Other changes
We are 
-	moving the results from CIFAR-10 into the main paper from the appendix with the extra page made available
-	adding results from a vanilla LeNet and HB-CNN (i.e no smoothing or noise in training data) for MNIST
-	assuming sufficient space, moving the ablation results into Figure 3 from the appendix
-	making improvements to how we show the inclusion of unpooling and gradient unpooling in the models, and how we matched for parameter numbers for the size-controlled CNN 
-	adding details about the hyperparamters used for our adversarial attacks
